extracted.intended_audience: performers, producers and others considering participation in the Edinburgh Festival Fringe (and researchers of the festival)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and de facto standards for participating in and being evaluated at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, covering the Fringe's open-access ethos, registration and venue requirements, costs and business models, controversies, review dynamics, and awards eligibility. Useful for artists planning a show and for those seeking to understand how work is judged and recognised at the Fringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open access / unjuried festival principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fringe is an open access festival; the Fringe Society 'did not come together so that groups could be invited, or in some way artistically vetted. What was performed and how it was done was left entirely to each Fringe group.' This approach is sometimes referred to as an unjuried festival, open access arts festival or a fringe festival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for producers: the festival does not perform artistic vetting — you are free to present what you choose. Anti-pattern: expecting selection or curation by Fringe Society. Context: this is central to debates about quality at the Fringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration and venue requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in the Fringe requires registration, payment of a registration fee, and use of a Fringe venue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 2008 registration fee was £289.05. Outdoor spaces (e.g., parts of the Royal Mile) may also require registration. Some artists choose to perform outside Fringe auspices to avoid these requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fringe Society vision and values
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fringe Society's vision: 'to give anyone a stage and everyone a seat.' Three values established to guide behaviours and decisions: 'Celebrate performing arts; Be open to all; Look out for each other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are normative expectations for stakeholders (artists, venues, residents, government bodies) and guide festival policy and messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free / pay-what-you-can business models
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative models exist (Free Fringe, The Laughing Horse Free Edinburgh Fringe Festival, Forest Fringe, 'Pay What You Want' initiatives) which aim to reduce costs for performers and audiences by not charging for space and/or collecting donations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: reduce financial barrier to participation and attendance. Example guidance: Forest Fringe provided no-cost space and accommodation in some years. Use-case: producers seeking low-cost entry or audience-building. Anti-pattern: confusing 'free' with lack of quality — many free shows are professional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs to performers
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting on a show at the Fringe can be costly due to registration fees, venue hire, accommodation, travel and marketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should budget for registration, venue guarantees/rents, theatre licence fees, accommodation and marketing. Independent/free venues can reduce costs. Negotiation with big venues is increasingly possible. Example: rising venue and licence costs have been cited as drivers of higher ticket prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs to venues / theatre licence fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Running a venue at the Fringe is costly: theatre licence fees rose dramatically (by 2009 they had risen 800% in the preceding three years), starting at around £824 for venues up to 200 people and rising to £2,472 for venues up to 5,000 people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These costs can be punitive to smaller venues and site-specific performances; venues must account for these fees when setting guarantees and ticket pricing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay-to-play / advance charging by venues (criticised practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some venues charge acts to perform in advance of the Fringe (venue rents/guarantees, compulsory marketing and various deductions), which can mean performers are charged more than they can make back in ticket sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice has been widely criticised as commercialising the Fringe; anti-pattern: agreeing to onerous guarantees or deductions without clear return. Response example: Heroes of Fringe (Bob Slayer) was set up as a statement against Pay-To-Play venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter freedom and resulting controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: The freedom to put on any show has periodically produced controversy over sexual explicitness or religion, sometimes bringing performers into conflict with local councillors and leading to censorship in certain cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organisers defend the Fringe as an open platform; producers should be aware controversy can be used as publicity but also risks censorship or political pushback. Example: festival contacted Mark Meechan to clarify his status when his publicity implied a ban.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of comedy's dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy has grown to become the largest section of the Fringe programme (first overtook theatre in 2008), prompting criticism that this 'domination by comedy' has changed the nature of the Fringe and marginalised non-comedy events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers in non-comedy genres should note audience composition and programming pressures; programmers/venues may privilege comedy. Anti-pattern: assuming audience tastes mirror pre-2008 distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work and pay conditions scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns have raised awareness of and challenged alleged poor working conditions during the Fringe (supported by City of Edinburgh Council and Unite the Union). Fringe leadership has sometimes contested criticisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers and venues should consider fair pay and working conditions as reputational and regulatory risks; aligning with 'Fair Fringe' principles can attract support and avoid criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviews as a route to success
rubrics_metrics.description: A favourable review is often the ultimate goal for many groups, helping to minimise financial losses and provide kudos. Historically, The Scotsman aimed to review every show; now reviewers are selective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeting prominent reviewers (The Scotsman, The Guardian, The Independent, The Stage, specialist Fringe outlets like ThreeWeeks, Broadway Baby, Chortle, Fest, The List) can materially affect a show's profile and box office. The British Comedy Guide collates comedy reviews; volume of reviews varies by outlet and year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fringe First awards eligibility (The Scotsman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fringe First awards were established to encourage new theatre writing and are 'given only to new plays (or new translations)'. Several are awarded each week of the Fringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers of new writing should highlight novelty to be eligible; the award offers prestige for playwrights and companies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Herald Angels / Archangels awards criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Herald Angels and Archangels are awarded by The Herald's arts writers to performers or shows 'deemed worthy of recognition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are editorial awards given each week; submission is not a formal application process like a juried prize, but visibility to The Herald's writers is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage Awards for Acting Excellence criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The Stage Awards are given for acting excellence (around a dozen awards each year) and include a Special Award for distinctive contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting quality and standout performances are central; technical and ensemble achievements may be recognised via Special Awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total Theatre Awards focus and public Wild Card
rubrics_metrics.description: Total Theatre Awards recognise excellence in physical and visual theatre; categories vary year to year and include a Wild Card award chosen by the festival-going public (added in 2007).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical/visual theatre makers should target Total Theatre; public-engaged elements can help secure the Wild Card.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amnesty International Freedom of Expression Award
rubrics_metrics.description: An award introduced in 2002 recognising performances that uphold or challenge issues of freedom of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows dealing with human-rights themes or controversial speech may be considered; nomination/selection processes are editorial/curatorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carol Tambor Best of Edinburgh Award eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible a show must have received a four or five star rating in The Scotsman and must not have previously played in New York; the prize is to put the show on in New York.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This award is explicitly for highly-rated productions that have not already had a New York run; producers seeking transfer opportunities should note these eligibility gates.

rubrics_metrics.name: ThreeWeeks Editors' Awards selection criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: ThreeWeeks Editors' Awards are given to the ten things that have most excited the ThreeWeeks editors each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are editorially curated selections — strive for surprise, innovation or notable moments that catch editors' attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadway Baby 'Bobby' and 'Technical Bobby' awards criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bobby (launched 2011) is given to the best shows of the festival as decided by the Broadway Baby judging panel; a Technical Bobby recognises technical achievement (lighting, set design).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical excellence can be the basis for recognition distinct from overall show awards; panels judge across many entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malcolm Hardee Awards categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Malcolm Hardee Awards have categories: Comic Originality, Cunning Stunt and Act Most Likely To Make A Million Quid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These awards value originality, stunt-based publicity/innovation, and perceived commercial potential; they are an unconventional set of recognitions and can raise profile for distinctive acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funniest Joke of the Fringe selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Each year the Funniest Joke of the Fringe is awarded, along with a top-10 list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a publicity-focused recognition for single jokes; comedians seeking viral/press attention may aim for standout one-liners or memorable punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards and recognition are diverse and genre-specific
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a growing number of awards across drama, comedy and technical fields (Fringe Firsts, Herald Angels, Stage Awards, Total Theatre, Amnesty award, Carol Tambor, ThreeWeeks Editors' Awards, Bobby Awards, Malcolm Hardee Awards, Funniest Joke, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should identify which awards map to their genre/strengths and plan publicity/eligibility accordingly; different awards have distinct eligibility rules (e.g., new writing only, Scotsman ratings required, technical vs content awards).
